categories.name: Organization design and roles
categories.summary: Who does what, who decides, and who covers when someone is out. In a small practice a few people hold many roles, so the risk is not confusion but a function that stops when one person is away.
good_looks_like: A one-page chart shows every function, the person responsible and a named backup.
Each role has a short written list of duties and the decisions it may make alone.
Work done by vendors or software has a named person who checks it.
The chart is reviewed whenever someone joins, leaves or a vendor changes.
failure_modes: Only one person knows how payroll, credentialing or the billing system works, and that person leaves.
The owner spends hours on tasks a staff member could do at a fraction of the cost.
Two people each assume the other is following up denials or renewals.
A vendor's work is never checked because nobody owns the relationship.
key_questions: Could each critical function run for two weeks without its usual person?
Which tasks does the owner do that someone else could?
Who checks the work of each vendor and each automated process?
When was the list of roles last updated?

actions.detail: List functions down the page: clinical work, scheduling or census, billing, credentialing, payroll and finance, compliance, technology. Add an owner and a backup for each.
The backup performs the task at least once a quarter with the written procedure.
Each quarter, hand one recurring task to staff, a vendor or software, with a check.

actions.action: Name an owner for every vendor
actions.detail: One person receives the vendor's reports and reviews performance.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, and in those with fewer than five people the chart is mostly about backups. Practices with no front desk (hospital rounds, nursing facilities, home visits) still need a named owner for census tracking and charge capture, and any practice using a billing vendor or software agents needs a named person who oversees them.

vendor_refs.note: Defines the billing roles and suggests team structures by practice size. Useful as a function list. Team sizes have no source, and it assumes human staff or vendors only.
Lists the functions a billing team must own and staff counts by number of clinicians. The staff counts have no source.

categories.evidence_note: Standard management practice, reflected in the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) body of knowledge and the Baldrige workforce criteria from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. No measured benchmark applies.

metrics.name: Critical functions with a trained backup
metrics.definition: Share of the practice's critical functions for which a second person has the access, the written procedure and recent practice to perform it.
metrics.formula: Functions with a backup who performed the task in the last 6 months / critical functions
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100% for payroll, claim submission, credentialing and bank access.
metrics.data_hint: The function chart, reviewed each quarter.

categories.name: Hiring and onboarding
categories.summary: Finding, choosing and starting clinicians and staff. For clinicians the hidden constraint is time: payer enrollment takes weeks to months, and visits may go unpaid until it is done.
good_looks_like: Each opening has a written role, pay range and the three things the person must be able to do.
Enrollment paperwork starts at offer signing. The Medicare application is filed no more than 60 days before the start date, since earlier ones may be returned (42 CFR 424.526).
New hires get a written first-90-day plan and a named person to ask.
At least ten of a new clinician's first notes are reviewed for coding and documentation.
failure_modes: A clinician sees Medicare patients more than 30 days before the application is filed, and those visits can never be billed (42 CFR 424.520, 424.521).
A health plan's effective date turns out later than assumed, and the plan pays nothing for visits before it.
Hiring happens only after someone quits, so the practice runs short for months.
A new biller learns from the last biller's habits, including the wrong ones.
References and license or exclusion checks are skipped for a familiar candidate.
key_questions: How long did our last hire take from posting to start, and from start to full productivity?
For our last clinician, how many days passed between start date and the first payable visit for each payer?
Do we check the license, references and the federal exclusion list before every offer?
Is there a written plan for a new person's first 90 days?

actions.action: Start enrollment work at offer acceptance
actions.detail: Collect documents with the signed offer and start health plan and Medicaid applications at once. File Medicare no more than 60 days before the start date and before the first visit. Track each application weekly.

Verify the license with the state board, search the federal exclusion list (people barred from Medicare and Medicaid) and any state Medicaid list, and call references. Recheck the lists periodically, as the Office of Inspector General (OIG) advises.
Systems access, training, shadowing, first tasks, and check-ins at 30, 60 and 90 days.

actions.action: Audit a new clinician's first notes
actions.detail: Review at least 10 notes in the first month for visit level, documentation and place of service. The OIG's guide for a routine audit is five to ten records per physician.

categories.applies_when: Any practice that hires: First Coast, Florida's Medicare contractor, lists standards of 15 days for 95% of complete online applications and 50 days for 95% of those needing follow-up, and each health plan sets its own timeline. Clinicians who work in hospitals or other facilities need privileges or the facility's own credentialing before the first visit (hospitals: 42 CFR 482.22).

vendor_refs.note: Interview and reference-check questions that test billing habits. Useful. It says nothing about license, background or exclusion screening.
Pre-hire skills test and an onboarding plan with full review of early work, then spot checks. Sensible. The review percentages are the vendor's own.

Advises starting credentialing 90 days ahead and billing under a supervising clinician's number meanwhile. Risky: Medicare permits that only for supervised office care, never in hospitals or skilled nursing facilities.

categories.evidence_note: Medicare's filing and effective-date rules are federal regulation. Processing standards are published by the Medicare contractor. Health plan timelines vary by contract and are not published. Screening follows Office of Inspector General guidance. Other hiring practices are professional judgment.

metrics.name: Days to fill an open position
metrics.definition: Calendar days from the decision to hire to the person's first day.
metrics.formula: Start date - date the opening was approved
metrics.benchmark_note: No benchmark for staff or small practices was found. The Association for Advancing Physician and Provider Recruitment reported 2023 physician medians of 77 to 228 days by specialty from search start to signed contract, in about 150 health organizations. Track your own trend.

metrics.name: New hires still employed after 12 months
metrics.definition: Share of people hired in a period who are still with the practice one year after their start date.
metrics.formula: Hires still employed at 12 months / hires in the period
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. In a small practice count people, not percentages: each early departure is worth a review.

categories.name: Clinician compensation design
categories.summary: How physicians and advanced practice clinicians (nurse practitioners and physician assistants) are paid: salary, productivity, quality incentives, and pay for call or directorships. The plan should be affordable, legal, and reward what the practice needs.
good_looks_like: The plan fits on one page and each clinician can calculate their own pay.
Total pay is compared each year with a named survey for the specialty.
Productivity is measured in work relative value units (RVUs), Medicare's score for the clinician's work in each service, which does not change with payer mix.
Incentives reward personally performed work or quality, never the volume or value of a clinician's referrals for tests, therapy or other billed services.
The plan states which year's Medicare work values it counts and who gets credit for care management and shared visits.
failure_modes: Pay tied to collections punishes clinicians for the payer mix and for billing office errors.
A productivity plan with no audit rewards higher visit levels, and levels drift upward.
Guaranteed salaries exceed what the clinician's work brings in, and nobody has done the arithmetic.
A bonus that rises with a physician's referrals for lab, imaging or therapy services can break the federal self-referral law (42 CFR 411.352 and 411.357).
A nursing facility pays a clinician as medical director with no written agreement or time log, so the pay can look like payment for referrals.
key_questions: What does each clinician cost in total, and what do they collect?
How does each clinician's pay per work unit compare with the survey median?
Does any part of pay depend on referrals or on services the clinician does not personally perform?
Is every clinician's level mix audited at least yearly?
Is any clinician paid by a facility or vendor that also sends us patients or receives our referrals?

actions.action: Calculate cost and collections per clinician
actions.detail: Total pay with taxes and benefits against collections attributable to that clinician, each year.

Compare with a named survey median for the specialty and record the source. Note which year's Medicare work values you used: in 2026 Medicare cut the work values of most non-time-based services, such as procedures, by 2.5%.

actions.action: Pair productivity pay with a coding audit
actions.detail: Any plan that pays more for more work units needs an independent audit of levels.

actions.action: Have counsel review incentive and director terms
actions.detail: Bonuses and medical director pay must fit the self-referral and kickback rules. A directorship should have a written agreement, fair market pay set in advance and a log of hours worked.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with more than one clinician, and solo owners setting their own salary. Medicare pays nurse practitioners and physician assistants 85% of the physician rate (42 CFR 414.56, 414.52), and its facility rate for most services is lower than its office rate, so facility-based practices should test survey pay rates against what their own visits collect.

vendor_refs.note: Explains four pay models and how each fails. Its benchmark table is constructed, far below survey medians, and it overstates the self-referral rules, including a supposed cap on owner pay.
Written for a physician weighing a job offer. Useful as the list of questions a hire will ask. Its pay-per-work-unit range has no source, and it omits nurse practitioner pay.

categories.evidence_note: Survey medians are measured but come mostly from large groups, and free surveys such as Doximity's report self-reported averages. The self-referral and kickback limits on pay are federal regulation. Plan design itself is judgment.

metrics.name: Compensation per work RVU
metrics.definition: Total cash compensation for a clinician divided by the work relative value units (RVUs) of the services that clinician personally performed.
metrics.formula: Total compensation / work RVUs personally performed
metrics.benchmark_typical: about $53 family medicine, $56 internal medicine, $34 primary care nurse practitioner
metrics.benchmark_note: AMGA (American Medical Group Association) 2026 survey medians, 2025 data, from 451 medical groups and health systems, mostly large. A reference point, not a target. A figure far below the median can mean unusually high billed work units, so check the coding.
metrics.data_hint: Payroll for pay. The billing system for services by rendering clinician, multiplied by the Medicare work value of each code.
metrics.vendor_claim: Pay per work RVU runs $45 to $55 in primary care and $45 to $65 nationally, and each clinician's effective rate should sit within 15% of the benchmark.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Partly supported. AMGA's 2025 primary care medians ($52.61, $55.62) sit near the top of that range, surgical specialties run higher, and the 15% rule has no source.

metrics.name: Clinician compensation as a share of collections
metrics.definition: Total pay and benefits of all clinicians, including a market wage for owners, as a share of professional collections.
metrics.formula: (Clinician pay, payroll taxes and benefits, with a market wage for owners) / professional collections
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. For context, the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) reports support staff cost at roughly 30% to 34% of revenue at the median (2025 data). Compare with your own trend: clinician cost plus all other costs must leave a margin.
metrics.vendor_claim: Provider pay should run 45% to 55% of net revenue, with over 60% a warning sign.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. The library names no source, year or definition of whose pay counts, and the association's cost tables are paywalled.

categories.name: Staff pay and incentives
categories.summary: Pay, raises, benefits and bonuses for non-clinician staff. Medical receptionist and medical assistant pay rose more than 20% in the five years to 2025, so pay ranges must be checked against the local market each year.
good_looks_like: Each role has a pay range based on local market data, reviewed yearly.
Raises follow a stated rule tied to performance and market movement.
Any bonus rewards accurate, complete work, such as claims paid on first submission, not dollars billed or collected.
Benefits are priced and communicated as part of total pay.
Bonuses promised in advance are counted in the overtime rate of hourly staff (29 CFR 778.211).
failure_modes: The best employee leaves for two dollars an hour more because nobody checked the market.
A bonus on charges or claims submitted rewards speed over accuracy.
Long-serving staff are paid less than new hires for the same job.
Overtime is paid routinely because the workload was never matched to staffing.
key_questions: When did we last compare each role's pay with local wages?
Is any staff bonus tied to dollars billed?
What would it cost to replace our most important staff member?
How much overtime did we pay last quarter?

actions.action: Check pay against the market yearly
actions.detail: Use a published survey or current local job postings for each role, and record what you found.

actions.action: Tie incentives to quality of work
actions.detail: Use accuracy and timeliness measures. Never pay billing staff a share of charges. Put the bonus rule in writing and include promised bonuses when calculating overtime.
Persistent overtime is a staffing or process problem.

categories.applies_when: Practices with employed staff, including remote billing or care coordination staff where there is no front desk. Practices that outsource billing or use automation have fewer roles but depend more on each one.

vendor_refs.note: Pay bands for billing roles with location and certification adjustments, plus bonus designs to avoid. The pay figures have no source, two tables disagree, and overtime rules are missing.

categories.evidence_note: The Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) publishes staff pay data, mostly behind a paywall, and the figures cited are from its free reports. The overtime rule for bonuses is federal regulation. Incentive design is professional guidance.

metrics.name: Staff pay against the local market
metrics.definition: Each role's pay rate as a percentage of the local market median for that role.
metrics.formula: Role pay rate / local market median for the role
metrics.benchmark_note: No published standard for where pay should sit against the market was found. Compare each role with the local median yearly. MGMA reports five-year pay growth to 2025 of 22.0% for medical receptionists and 20.6% for medical assistants, so old ranges are likely stale.
metrics.data_hint: Payroll, compared with a wage survey or current local postings.
metrics.vendor_claim: Flag any role paid more than 10% below the market median, after adjusting for location and specialty, as a retention risk.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given for the 10% line, and the library's own pay tables are unsourced.

categories.name: Productivity, accountability and performance
categories.summary: Clear expectations for each role, a regular look at whether they are met, and a conversation when they are not. For automated work, the same idea applies: a standard, a log and a review.
good_looks_like: Each role has two or three measurable standards, such as claims worked per day or denials touched within 48 hours.
Work queues show what is waiting and how old it is, every day.
Every person has a written review at least once a year.
Automated processes have a run log and a monthly human sample.
failure_modes: Nobody notices a queue growing until receivables have aged by a month.
Performance problems are discussed for the first time at termination.
Activity is measured, such as calls made, while results are not.
Software runs unattended and its errors are found by a payer.
key_questions: What are the two measures that tell us each role is being done well?
How old is the oldest item in each work queue today?
Has every person had a written review in the last 12 months?
Who reviews what our automated processes did last month?

actions.action: Set two or three standards per role
actions.detail: Choose measures of results the person controls, and review them monthly.
Oldest item and count for charges, rejections, denials, unposted payments and credentialing.
Once a year at minimum, with a short quarterly check-in.
Review a fixed number of automated actions each month against the source record.

categories.applies_when: Every practice: with in-house billing staff the measures are per person, with a billing company they become contract service levels, and with software agents they are run logs and a sampled review. For clinicians who round in facilities or visit homes, the key standard is every visit documented and its charge entered within a set number of days.

vendor_refs.note: Written standards per role, a weekly metrics meeting and documented coaching. A usable routine. Its targets and the medians it attributes to two trade associations have no traceable source.
Role scorecard with targets and intervention levels, and weekly, monthly and quarterly reviews. Targets are unsourced, and its charge-entry standard shifts between 24 and 48 hours.
Uses claims per full-time person and the share of staff time spent on rework as diagnostics. A good idea, but its 750 to 1,200 claims benchmark has no source.

categories.evidence_note: Management practice. The few measured productivity figures come from the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) and vary with role definitions. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) defines revenue cycle measures but publishes no targets.

metrics.name: Staff with a performance review in the last 12 months
metrics.definition: Share of employees who have had a written review within the past year.
metrics.formula: Employees reviewed in the last 12 months / employees
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is everyone.

metrics.name: Claims or accounts worked per billing full-time equivalent
metrics.definition: Output of billing staff per full-time person, in claims submitted, accounts followed up or encounters coded per day.
metrics.formula: Units of work completed / full-time equivalents / working days
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA's 2023 report (2022 data, single-specialty practices): coding staff processed 41 encounters a day, down from 75 in 2019. No public figure for claims per biller was found. Definitions differ, so compare with your own trend.
metrics.data_hint: Billing system productivity reports by user.
metrics.vendor_claim: An outpatient billing team should process 750 to 1,200 claims per full-time person a month, and 400 signals a problem.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is named. The only public figure found is in another unit: 41 encounters coded per coder per day in 2022 (MGMA).

categories.name: Training and competency
categories.summary: What each person must know to do the job correctly, taught at hire and refreshed every year. Coding rules change annually, clinicians choose most codes themselves, and Medicare's 2025 review found improper payment rates of 5% to 14% for common visit types.
good_looks_like: New staff and clinicians are trained on the systems, privacy rules and the practice's billing rules before working alone.
Clinicians receive coding education each year, built from their own audit results.
Procedure code and Medicare fee changes are reviewed each December and diagnosis code changes each September, before they take effect.
Staff exposed to blood or body fluids get bloodborne pathogen training at assignment and every year (29 CFR 1910.1030).
Training is recorded: who, what, when.
failure_modes: Clinicians last learned visit coding in residency, before the rules changed.
A code is deleted on January 1 and the practice keeps billing it for weeks.
Privacy training was done once at hire and never again.
There is no record of training when an auditor asks for it.
key_questions: When did each clinician last receive coding education specific to our visit types?
Who reviews the annual code and Medicare payment changes for us?
Can we show a record of privacy and compliance training for everyone?
Does anyone on the team, or an outside reviewer, hold a coding certification?

actions.detail: After each chart audit, a one-hour session on the patterns found, for all clinicians.

actions.action: Review code and fee changes before they start
actions.detail: Each December, summarize new, deleted and revised procedure codes and the Medicare final rule on one page. Each September, do the same for diagnosis codes, which change October 1.
Date, topic, attendees and materials, kept with the compliance files. Privacy training must be documented (45 CFR 164.530).
Each backup performs the task once a quarter, following the written procedure.

categories.applies_when: Every practice: where billing is outsourced or automated, clinicians still choose the codes and need the training, and someone inside must understand enough to supervise. For clinicians who work in hospitals, nursing facilities or homes, training covers place of service, facility visit codes and required visit schedules instead of front-desk topics.

vendor_refs.note: Calls for yearly coding-update training for all billing staff and support for coder certification. Sound. Its claim that certification measurably improves first-pass claim results has no source.

categories.evidence_note: Office of Inspector General (OIG) guidance lists training among seven compliance program elements and expects it at hire and at least yearly. Privacy training (45 CFR 164.530) and bloodborne pathogen training (29 CFR 1910.1030) are federal rules. Other content is the practice's choice.

metrics.name: Training hours per person per year
metrics.definition: Recorded hours of job, coding, privacy and compliance training for each clinician and staff member in a year.
metrics.benchmark_red: under 1 hour a year per person
metrics.benchmark_note: A floor, not a target. OIG's 2000 guidance for small practices says its settlement agreements usually require at least one hour a year of basic compliance training, and it recommends yearly coding and billing training. No benchmark for total hours was found.

categories.name: Retention, culture and well-being
categories.summary: Keeping the people the practice depends on, and noticing overload before it becomes a resignation. Replacing a clinician can mean months of lost revenue, and about four in ten physicians report a symptom of burnout.
good_looks_like: Turnover is counted each year by role, and every departure has an exit conversation.
Workload is looked at directly: visits per day, after-hours charting, calls and, for clinicians who visit facilities or homes, travel time.
Clinicians have protected time off with real coverage.
The owner's own workload and health are treated as a business risk.
failure_modes: A key person resigns and the reasons were known for a year.
The owner covers every gap personally until the owner becomes the gap.
After-hours documentation grows unnoticed.
Good work is never acknowledged, only errors.
key_questions: Who left in the last two years, and why?
How many hours a week does each clinician chart after hours?
When did each clinician, including the owner, last take a full week off?
What would make our most important person leave?

actions.action: Count turnover and hold exit conversations
actions.detail: Record role, tenure and reason for every departure.
A short private conversation or survey on workload, after-hours work and obstacles, including the owner's own.

actions.action: Arrange real coverage for time off
actions.detail: A written arrangement so that vacation is not followed by a backlog.

actions.action: Agree a retention plan for key people
actions.detail: For anyone whose loss would cut revenue sharply: pay review, schedule, growth path.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, and in very small ones each departure is a crisis, so keeping one or two key people matters more than a turnover percentage. For clinicians who travel between facilities or homes, drive time and after-hours calls from facility staff count as workload.

vendor_refs.note: Retention levers and a knowledge audit to run before anyone leaves. Useful. Its figure that replacing a biller costs 50% to 100% of salary has no source.

categories.evidence_note: Turnover medians are measured by the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) and burnout rates by the American Medical Association (AMA). Both samples are dominated by larger organizations.

metrics.name: Annual staff turnover
metrics.definition: Departures during the year as a share of average headcount, counted by role group.
metrics.benchmark_red: at or above the 2022 peak: 40% front office, 33% clinical support
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA single-specialty medians, 2025 data. The red line is the 2022 level, which MGMA called exceptionally high. It is our reading, not a published threshold. In a small practice one departure moves the rate a lot, so count people.
metrics.vendor_claim: Keep yearly staff retention on a billing team above 80%, with under 70% as the level that needs action.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given. MGMA's 2025 median turnover for business office staff was 0%, so a typical practice already beats the 80% goal.

metrics.name: Clinicians reporting burnout
metrics.definition: Share of clinicians who report at least one symptom of burnout on a short validated survey question.
metrics.benchmark_typical: about 42% of physicians in a 2025 health-system sample
metrics.benchmark_note: AMA Organizational Biopsy, 2025 data: 41.9% of nearly 19,000 physicians at 106 health systems reported at least one symptom, and 45% in family medicine. No small-practice figure was found. In a practice of a few clinicians, ask each one directly.
metrics.data_hint: A one-question annual survey or a direct conversation.

categories.name: Employment agreements and HR compliance
categories.summary: The contracts and employment rules that apply to clinicians and staff: written agreements, restrictive covenants such as non-competes, wage and hour law, employee or contractor status, personnel files and workplace safety.
good_looks_like: Every clinician has a signed, current agreement covering pay, duties, term, termination and malpractice tail.
Advanced practice clinicians have whatever supervision or collaboration document the state requires.
Staff are correctly classed for overtime, and contractors truly are contractors under the tax tests.
Personnel files hold license checks, training records and required forms.
Where staff handle blood or sharps, a written exposure control plan exists and is reviewed yearly (29 CFR 1910.1030).
failure_modes: A clinician works for years on an expired or unsigned agreement.
A non-compete is unenforceable as written, or enforceable against the owner in a way nobody intended.
A long-time contractor is really an employee under the tax tests, and the practice owes back employment taxes.
Nobody knows who pays for malpractice tail coverage when a clinician leaves.
A salaried employee who does not meet the federal exemption tests is owed back overtime.
key_questions: Does every clinician have a signed agreement that matches how they are actually paid?
What happens to patients, records and tail coverage if a clinician leaves?
Are our advanced practice clinicians' state-required protocols signed and current?
Has anyone reviewed how we classify each worker?

actions.detail: Check pay terms, term dates, covenants and tail coverage against current practice.
Supervision or collaboration agreements, signed, kept where the state requires and updated when clinicians or sites change.
State law decides what is enforceable and for how long.
Review each contractor against the Internal Revenue Service tests: who controls the work, who bears the business costs, and how the relationship is set up. Document the reasoning.

actions.action: Check overtime status of salaried staff
actions.detail: A salaried employee is exempt from overtime only if the job duties qualify and the salary is at or above the federal threshold (29 CFR 541.600). State law may be stricter.

categories.applies_when: Every practice with clinicians or staff other than the owner, under state law that varies widely. In Florida, for example, a covenant against a former employee is presumed reasonable at six months or less and unreasonable over two years (section 542.335), and a nurse practitioner needs a written physician protocol unless registered for autonomous primary care practice (sections 464.012, 464.0123).

vendor_refs.note: Lists the contract terms a clinician will question: covenant radius and length, tail coverage, bonus repayment. It says courts read vague non-competes against the employer, which Florida's statute forbids.
Stresses written, signed, current agreements. Sound practice, but it wrongly says every arrangement needs a one-year written contract and that an expired agreement loses protection.

categories.evidence_note: Covenant rules are state statute. A federal court set aside the rule that would have banned most non-competes in 2024, and it was removed from the federal regulations in February 2026. Worker classification, overtime and workplace safety rules are federal and state law.

metrics.name: Clinicians and key staff with a signed, current agreement
metrics.definition: Share of clinicians and key staff whose written agreement is signed, unexpired and matches their current pay and duties.
metrics.formula: People with a current signed agreement / clinicians and key staff
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.
metrics.vendor_claim: Every compensation arrangement should sit in a written, signed, unexpired agreement.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Supported as good practice. The library overstates the law: the federal self-referral rules require a writing for contractor arrangements, not for employees.

categories.name: Outsourcing versus in-house
categories.summary: Whether billing, coding, credentialing, bookkeeping and technology are done by employees, by a vendor, or by software. Each model trades cost against control, and the practice stays responsible for the result in all of them.
good_looks_like: The practice knows its full cost for each function under the current model.
Any vendor contract states service levels, reporting, data ownership and how to leave.
Someone inside the practice understands the work well enough to judge it.
Results are compared before and after any change of model.
failure_modes: A percentage-of-collections vendor works the easy claims and lets the hard ones age.
The practice cannot get its own data back when it wants to leave.
Work is brought in-house or automated to save money, and nobody is left who can check it.
The owner believes responsibility for claims moved to the vendor. It did not.
A billing company paid a percentage of collections receives Medicare payments in its own account, which federal rules forbid (42 CFR 424.73, 424.80).
key_questions: What does each function cost us now, as a share of collections?
What do our vendor contracts say about data, reporting and termination?
Who inside the practice reviews the vendor's or the software's work?
What happened to net collections and receivables after our last change?

actions.action: Calculate the full cost of each model
actions.detail: Include staff time, software, clearinghouse fees and the owner's oversight time.

actions.action: Put service levels in the contract
actions.detail: Days to submit, denial follow-up time, monthly reports, data return on exit, and the business associate agreement the privacy rule requires (45 CFR 164.502). Medicare payments go to an account the practice controls.
An outside coding audit and a monthly look at receivables and denials, whatever the model.

actions.action: Measure before and after any change
actions.detail: Net collection rate, days in receivables and denial rate for six months each side. For scale, billing companies reported mean net collection of 85% for office practices in a 2024 trade survey.

categories.applies_when: Every practice makes this choice for billing and usually for bookkeeping, payroll and technology. Practices that automate with software agents face the same questions with a different vendor, and facility-based practices should confirm that a vendor knows facility visit and place-of-service rules.

vendor_refs.note: Fee models, contract clauses to negotiate, a monthly monitoring form and an exit plan. Useful. Fee ranges and contract floors are unsourced, and Medicare's billing agent rule is missing.
Defines cost to collect and compares in-house with vendor cost alongside net collection rate. A sound method. Its 4% to 6% target band has no source.
Advises deciding build, buy or outsource one function at a time. Gives no costs for any option and no option to automate.

categories.evidence_note: Fee ranges come from a 2010 trade article and are repeated without newer data. Office of Inspector General (OIG) guidance from 2000 says physicians remain responsible for claims a billing service sends in their name. The billing agent payment rule is federal regulation.

metrics.name: Outsourced billing fee as a share of collections
metrics.definition: What the practice pays a billing company, as a percentage of the collections that company handles.
metrics.formula: Billing vendor fees / collections handled by the vendor
metrics.benchmark_typical: 4% to 5% high-payment specialties, 8% to 10% primary care (2010 figures)
metrics.benchmark_note: Physicians Practice, 2010, the only traceable public figures. No current benchmark was found. Judge the fee together with net collection rate. For scale, one academic system measured all billing work, including physician time, at 14.5% of primary care professional revenue (JAMA, 2018).
